items.title: ShEPhERD-score: Fast, adaptable three-dimensional alignment of molecular features
items.license: arXiv API terms; metadata CC0
items.abstract: Three-dimensional (3D) molecular similarity scoring and alignment are widely employed in ligand-based virtual screening and molecular design, and are increasingly used for training and evaluating machine learning models. Existing open-source methods utilize various molecular representations spanning shape, electrostatics, pharmacophores, and hybrid representations, but their implementations as independent software packages with distinct application programming interfaces (APIs), optimizers, and limited GPU support make them difficult to compare, combine, or extend. Here, we develop ShEPhERD-score into a unified, modular platform for differentiable 3D molecular similarity scoring and alignment by combining diverse molecular representations with high-performance Numba CPU and Triton GPU kernels to support both large-scale library screening and pairwise similarity workflows. In matched comparisons with open-source 3D similarity tools on the DUDE-Z virtual screening benchmark, ShEPhERD-score performed comparably or better in eight of nine cases. Across the scoring modes in ShEPhERD-score, throughput ranges from 17,800 to 1.03 million alignments/second for ten-million-conformer libraries using a single NVIDIA L40S GPU. Moreover, we found that the most effective scoring mode varied by protein target, indicating that target-specific calibration against validation data may be valuable before large-scale screening and underscoring the need for a unified platform that provides diverse molecular representations. Together, these capabilities establish ShEPhERD-score as a single, extensible toolkit for rapid virtual screening and machine learning workflows.

items.title: Micrograph B-factor estimation via Wilson statistics
items.license: arXiv API terms; metadata CC0
items.abstract: The single-particle cryo-electron microscopy imaging process is known to cause exponential decay in the amplitude and power spectra of proteins. This decay is modeled by the B factor and is currently corrected as a post-processing stage of the 3D reconstruction. As a consequence, all experimental images in the dataset are assumed to share the same B factor. In this paper, we suggest a novel approach wherein the B factor is determined and corrected as a preprocessing step to the reconstruction. We show such an approach can improve reconstruction resolution.

items.title: ST-FateFlow: Continuous Gene-Spatial Reconstruction with Differentiation-Potential Learning from Time-Resolved Spatial Transcriptomics
items.license: arXiv API terms; metadata CC0
items.abstract: Time-resolved spatial transcriptomics provides a powerful view of dynamic biological processes by measuring cellular states together with their spatial organization across time. However, destructive profiling and experimental cost restrict observations to a few discrete time points collected from independent samples, with no known cell pairing across time. This makes it difficult to reconstruct gene expression and tissue organization at unobserved stages and to characterize differentiation-associated dynamics. Here, we introduce ST-FateFlow, a flow-matching framework for continuous gene-spatial dynamics and differentiation-potential learning. ST-FateFlow jointly learns gene-expression and spatial-coordinate velocity fields, enabling interpolation of missing time points and continuous modeling of transcriptional evolution and tissue remodeling. In parallel, it independently learns a time-conditioned differentiation potential, whose values organize cell states along inferred differentiation progressions and support the analysis of differentiation-associated transcriptional changes. Across multiple time-resolved spatial transcriptomics datasets, ST-FateFlow effectively captures coordinated gene-expression and spatial dynamics. Case studies further show that the learned potential landscapes are consistent with known developmental and regenerative trajectories and help identify candidate genes associated with differentiation progression.

Given this low intrinsic copying fidelity, plausible scenarios for the spontaneous emergence of molecular evolution require an accuracy-enhancing mechanism. The mechanism exploits the observation that initial errors in template-directed polymerization of both DNA and RNA are likely to trigger a cascade of consecutive errors and significantly stall downstream extension. items.title: Blood-derived dietary protein promotes sleep in the mosquito Aedes aegypti
items.license: CC BY 4.0
items.abstract: Sleep is a ubiquitous, yet highly variable, behavior across species. The duration and timing of sleep are influenced by ecological demands and dietary context. In the mosquito Aedes aegypti , a blood-feeding insect with specialized nutritional requirements, the relationship between feeding and sleep remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated how blood-derived dietary protein influences sleep regulation. Using postural analysis, videography, and arousal-threshold assays, we established that immobility bouts of ≥10 min reliably define sleep in A. aegypti . Mosquitoes lacking the circadian clock gene cycle still maintained daily sleep rhythms but exhibited reduced sleep duration and heightened overall activity. Infrared activity monitoring revealed that blood-fed females showed a marked increase in sleep beginning immediately after feeding and persisting for several days, accompanied by reduced locomotor activity. Notably, this sleep elevation lasted well beyond the cessation of previously reported host-seeking phases, raising the possibility of distinct phases of opportunistic vs. targeted host pursuit. To determine the dietary basis of this effect, we tested mosquitoes fed a bovine serum albumin (BSA)-based diet. BSA feeding alone was sufficient to mimic the sleep-promoting and activity-reducing effects of blood, suggesting dietary protein is a major nutritional regulator.

items.title: Ramping-up hippocampal ripples and their neocortical coupling support human visual short-term memory
items.license: CC BY 4.0
items.abstract: Emerging evidence suggests that the hippocampus contributes to visual short-term memory (VSTM). However, the neural mechanisms through which hippocampal activity supports the maintenance of VSTM representations remain largely unknown. Here, using intracranial EEG recordings from human participants performing a delayed match-to-sample task for naturalistic objects, we investigated the role of hippocampal ripple activity—brief high-frequency oscillations associated with memory replay—in VSTM maintenance and hippocampal-neocortical communication. We found that hippocampal ripple rates progressively ramped up during the maintenance period and supported successful VSTM. More critically, hippocampal ripples were temporally coupled with the ripples in the lateral temporal lobe (LTL), and these coupled ripples were associated with memory reactivation in the LTL. These findings provide direct evidence that hippocampal–neocortical interaction via coupled ripples supports VSTM, extending the role of hippocampal ripples from long-term consolidation to short-term mnemonic processes and offering new insights into the dynamic coding mechanisms of working memory.

items.title: Rethinking laboratory sustainability
items.license: CC BY 4.0
items.abstract: Green lab initiatives like My Green Lab and LEAF (Laboratory Efficiency Assessment Framework), are paving the way towards sustainable research by promoting resource efficiency, energy conservation, and waste reduction through behavioral changes. However, these initiatives focus almost exclusively on material consumption, overlooking deeper facets of scientific waste that stem from questionable research practices: the environmental cost of unnecessary or poorly designed experiments, discarded null results, unreproducible research, and distorted reporting. I argue that a more meaningful discussion of scientific sustainability must look beyond physical resource management to examine the scientific process itself; to rethink the questions we ask, the experiments we do, and how we communicate our findings. To build a truly sustainable scientific ecosystem, Green Lab initiatives must join forces with Open Science and research integrity movements to update not only the hardware, but also the software of science.

items.title: ITK deficiency protects against autoimmune pulmonary hemorrhage in mice by promoting amphiregulin-producing regulatory T cells
items.license: CC BY 4.0
items.abstract: Pulmonary hemorrhage (PH) is a life-threatening manifestation of systemic autoimmunity caused by immune-mediated disruption of the alveolar capillary barrier. Despite high mortality, the molecular checkpoints that shift destructive inflammation toward protective immune regulation remain poorly defined. Here, using a pristane-induced PH mouse model, we identify interleukin-2-inducible T-cell kinase (ITK) as a critical regulator of autoimmune lung injury. ITK deficiency ( Itk⁻ / ⁻ ) conferred near-complete protection from PH and associated multiorgan injury, accompanied by reduced proinflammatory monocytes and neutrophils and increased Foxp3 + regulatory T cells (Tregs). Adoptive transfer of Itk⁻ / ⁻ Tregs protected wild-type recipients from PH and suppressed systemic proinflammatory cytokines, identifying Tregs as key mediators of tissue protection. Mechanistically, lung Itk ⁻ / ⁻ Tregs exhibited increased amphiregulin, a mediator of tissue repair. Transcriptomic profiling further showed that ITK loss reprogrammed Tregs toward a metabolically and functionally enhanced state, with enrichment of oxidative phosphorylation, mTORC1, and STAT5 signaling, and tissue-repair programs. These findings establish ITK as a regulator of the balance between pulmonary injury and reparative immunity and support targeting the ITK axis in severe inflammatory lung disease.

items.license: CC BY 4.0

Furthermore, we found SUMOylation of GDI1 at a conserved site plays a crucial role in efferocytosis regulation in mammals. This study defines a previously unrecognized mechanism by which SUMOylation drives apoptotic cell clearance.

items.title: Rollout models of human planning with exact action probabilities
items.license: CC BY 4.0
items.abstract: by Jeroen Olieslagers, Wei Ji Ma One proposed mechanism for human planning is the mental simulation, or “rollout,” of potential action sequences to evaluate future outcomes. While rollout-based models have seen great success in artificial intelligence, cognitive models that describe how people use rollouts remain scarce, in part because they are difficult to fit to behavioral data. Existing methods rely on computationally intensive simulations that result in approximate, noisy estimates of latent planning parameters. We introduce ROSETTE (Rollouts with Stochastic Early Termination and Tractable Estimation), a rollout-based model for finite goal-directed tasks with absorbing goals that provides analytically tractable, simulation-free model fitting. ROSETTE treats planning as a sequence of mental simulations formalized as an absorbing Markov chain. The model deterministically accumulates analytically computed expected rollout evidence and performs a variable number of policy-update cycles. We fit ROSETTE to data from human participants in two multi-step planning tasks and found that it well accounted for a rich set of summary statistics of behavior. By making this specific class of absorbing-goal rollout models tractable, our framework provides a testable account of how people may simulate and evaluate possible futures.

items.license: CC BY 4.0 (verified on article pages; occasional CC0)
items.abstract: by Yuxiang Tan, Yingqiang Cai, Kuan Fan, Xiaowen Li, Guangyu Qiu Long-horizon vessel trajectory prediction for maritime traffic monitoring and route planning requires both a prompt response to manoeuvres and control of error accumulation. UnifiedInternalMoE combines a motion-prior residual expert with four temporal predictors in a separate checkpoint for each region and seed. Convex weights are fitted to validation predictions at 5, 10, and 60 min and interpolated to produce the complete future trajectory. A ten-seed comparison across four regions, together with capacity controls, learned gating, and internal ablations, evaluates the benefit of the heterogeneous combination and its sources. In a five-seed evaluation on an independent Finnish AIS subset, the fusion has the lowest mean average displacement error (ADE) at all six horizons, with ADE@60 of 1719.53±25.80 m; it does not consistently lead in long-horizon final displacement error (FDE) or frozen source-to-target transfer. These results support the applicability of the same architecture when retrained for different regions and its use as a forecasting reference for shore-based analysis of long-horizon motion trends. Its applicability remains limited by the number of independent vessels, regional distribution differences, and computational cost.
